{{Short description|Discrete population dynamics model}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=October 2019}}

[[File:Ricker bifurcation.png|400px|thumb|[[Bifurcation diagram]] of the Ricker model with carrying capacity of 1000]]
The '''Ricker model''', named after [[Bill Ricker]], is a classic discrete [[population model]] which gives the expected number ''N''<sub>&nbsp;''t''+1</sub> (or density) of individuals in generation ''t''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 as a function of the number of individuals in the previous generation,<ref>Ricker (1954)</ref>

: <math>N_{t+1} = N_t e^{r\left(1-\frac{N_t}{k}\right)}.\,</math>

Here ''r'' is interpreted as an intrinsic growth rate and ''k'' as the [[carrying capacity]] of the environment. Unlike some other models like the [[Logistic map]], the carrying capacity in the Ricker model is not a hard barrier that cannot be exceeded by the population, but it only determines the overall scale of the population. The Ricker model was introduced in 1954 by Ricker in the context of [[Fish stocks|stock]] and recruitment in [[fisheries]].

The model can be used to predict the number of fish that will be present in a fishery.<ref>de Vries et al.</ref><ref>Marland</ref> Subsequent work has derived the model under other assumptions such as [[scramble competition]],<ref>Brännström and Sumpter(2005)</ref> within-year resource limited competition<ref name=Geritz /> or even as the outcome of source-sink Malthusian patches linked by density-dependent dispersal.<ref name="Marcos Marvá"> Marvá et al (2009)</ref><ref name="Bravo de la Parra">Bravo de la Parra et al (2013)</ref> The Ricker model is a [[limiting case (mathematics)|limiting case]] of the [[Hassell model]]<ref name=Geritz>Geritz and Kisdi (2004)</ref> which takes the form

: <math>N_{t+1} = k_1 \frac{N_t}{ \left(1+k_2 N_t\right)^c}. </math>

When ''c''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1, the Hassell model is simply the [[Beverton–Holt model]].
